extracted.intended_audience: students learning to write proofs in Lean (CS 22 students, TAs, instructors)
extracted.subtask_description: Stylistic and practical guidance for writing clear, maintainable Lean proofs: naming identifiers, managing goals, and using consistent indentation so proofs are readable and avoid common errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good style / thoughtful structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Good style is essential to making both programs and proofs clear and understandable. Taking the time to thoughtfully structure proofs makes writing and debugging easier, yields better and faster help from TAs, and aids learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the motivations for using a proof assistant in this course is that systems like Lean help you see the structure of a proof as it unfolds, and good style will make this structure clearer and easier to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifier syntax rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifiers in Lean (variables, theorem names, functions, and the like) must begin with a lower-case or capital letter and can contain most non-whitespace Unicode characters (except for those that are reserved for infix operations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular, the hyphen cannot appear in Lean identifiers (note for people from Pyret/Racket).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming convention: data declarations (def) in camelCase
rubrics_metrics.description: Data declarations, like functions, numbers, and other named data declared using def, are typically named in camel case (e.g., myGreatNat or addAndSquare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use camelCase for defs so their purpose/role is clear and consistent across the codebase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming convention: theorems in snake_case and descriptive names
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems are written in snake case (e.g., add_two_two_eq_four or mul_comm). Theorem names generally reflect the key operations that appear in the theorem statement (e.g., mul_sub or mul_sub_eq_mul_sub_mul for k * (m - n) = (k * m) - (k * n)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose theorem names that capture the principal operations/facts in the statement so others can infer the theorem's content from its name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name variables according to their kind (values vs hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always bear in mind the kind of variable you are introducing when you name it. Variables corresponding to values, like natural numbers or integers, should be given names similar to those in a paper proof (e.g., n or m for natural numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps you and readers understand what values are on hand at a given stage of the proof and supports deciding next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis naming convention (prefix with h)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses should be given names beginning with h followed by the variables or facts to which they pertain: for instance, the hypothesis m = n would be appropriately named hmn (or heq or hm_eq_n if there were other hypotheses involving m and n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent hypothesis naming makes it substantially easier to understand the values and assumptions in your context. Inductive hypotheses are an exception and may be, or begin with, ih.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shadowing names
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid shadowing: do not introduce a variable or hypothesis with the same name as one that already exists. When this happens, the first variable or hypothesis becomes inaccessible—you'll no longer be able to refer to it by name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shadowed names show a dagger (✝) next to them in the context. Tactics like assumption may still find the original, but direct reference is lost; avoid shadowing to prevent confusion and bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming rules apply across tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: The naming rules apply whenever you're introducing names into your context, regardless of the tactic being used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics such as assume, fix, have, and eliminate also allow you to specify names to add to your context—use the same naming conventions consistently for all of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal management: focus active goal with braces
rubrics_metrics.description: While every proof starts with a single goal, many tactics will create additional goals. By default new goals appear sequentially and tactics only affect the topmost goal; therefore, you should always focus the goal on which you're actively working using the { } syntax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In general, any tactic that generates multiple goals should immediately be followed by braces. Using braces clarifies which tactics apply to which goal and makes the structure of the proof clearer (examples show a bad proof without braces and a clear version using braces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use line breaks with braces for clarity and Infoview behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Although examples sometimes omit line breaks after opening and before closing braces for compactness, including those line breaks when writing proofs is strongly advised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omitting the line breaks may make the Infoview behave confusingly while writing; include line breaks to keep the Infoview and proof structure clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation must be consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Lean requires consistent indentation in proofs and within any focused subgoals. If you change indentation levels between successive tactic lines, your proof will likely fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The error messages caused by indentation issues can be confusing, so be careful about correctly indenting your lines. The page gives explicit examples labeled 'Don't do this!' showing incorrect indentation and the kinds of errors that result.
